deep.reconstruction:
Context: this is the opening of the main body of Riemann's Nachlass paper 'Zwei allgemeine Lehrsätze über lineare Differentialgleichungen mit algebraischen Coefficienten' (dated 1857). The previous page is the preamble. This page sets up the global monodromy data of an n-tuple of functions.

(1) Hypotheses. y = (y_1,...,y_n)^T are functions of a complex variable x. They are finite and locally single-valued (analytically continuable) everywhere except at finitely many points a,b,c,...,g. Analytic continuation along a loop around any one of these points changes them by a constant linear substitution: y -> M y with M constant.

(2) Normalisation by a cut. Draw a closed Jordan curve L that passes through a,b,...,g in that cyclic order. It divides the sphere into two simply connected regions. Each contains no singular point, so in each region every y_i has a single-valued, continuous branch. Riemann fixes the branches on the region lying on the positive side of L as the reference values.

(3) Local monodromy matrices. A positive circuit of x about a sends y_nu to sum_{i=1}^n A^nu_i y_i (nu = 1..n). In modern terms, y -> A y with the n x n matrix A = (A^nu_i): nu is the row index, i the column index. Likewise B = (B^nu_i) for a circuit about b, ..., G = (G^nu_i) for a circuit about g.

(4) Notation. The vector (y_1,...,y_n) is written (y). The coefficient array is written (A), similarly (B),...,(G). The transformed system (sum_i A^1_i y_i, ..., sum_i A^n_i y_i) is written (A)(y), i.e. the matrix-vector product A y. The sentence breaks off ('so findet zwischen ...').

(5) Continuation on the next page (for orientation). It gives the relation (G)(F)...(B)(A) = (0), with (0) the identity substitution. The reason: continuing successively around all branch points along the positive side of L is equivalent to traversing the boundary of the other region. That boundary is contractible there, since the functions are single-valued in that region. So the product of the local monodromies is the identity. This is the defining relation of the fundamental group of the sphere minus k points, here in its monodromy representation.
errors: The functions are called 'einwerthig' (single-valued) for all complex x except a,...,g. This is literally false, since nontrivial monodromy makes them globally multivalued. What is meant is local single-valuedness or uniformity in each cut region, which the following sentences make precise. This is a wording slip, not a mathematical error; the reading of the word itself is slightly uncertain.

Composition-order subtlety (not an error, a convention). If continuation around a gives y -> A y in terms of the original branches, and the original branches then undergo B around b, the composite has matrix A·B in the ordinary product of the arrays (A^nu_i). Riemann's notation (B)(A)(y) on the next page is consistent only if (B)(A) denotes composition of substitutions acting on the variables (first A, then B), not the ordinary matrix product B·A. Monodromy is an anti-homomorphism in this row convention. The relation 'product = identity' holds either way, since a product of matrices equals the identity iff the reversed product of the same matrices does in the appropriate cyclically-equivalent form; specifically, M_1...M_k = I implies M_k...M_1 = I after inversion only up to ordering. Riemann's stated order therefore needs care, but the result is unaffected because his convention is self-consistent.

results.what: Setup of an n-tuple of functions with prescribed branch points and constant linear monodromy substitutions, normalised by a closed cut through all branch points
results.modern_name: Monodromy representation of a local system / Fuchsian system on P^1 minus k points (Riemann's 'Q-functions', the setting of the Riemann–Hilbert problem)
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann (1857 P-function paper; this Nachlass paper, published in Werke 1876)

results.what: Matrix notation (A)(y) for linear substitutions and their composition
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann (in this context); matrix calculus formally Cayley 1858

deep.surprise_reason: This page is the beginning of Riemann's known Nachlass paper 'Zwei allgemeine Lehrsätze über lineare Differentialgleichungen mit algebraischen Coefficienten', printed in the Gesammelte Werke (1876). The monodromy setup and the relation it leads to are well known as Riemann's and are a standard part of the history of the Riemann–Hilbert problem. The page only sets up the definitions.

checkable.sympy: from sympy import *; x,a,b=symbols('x a b'); y=x**a*(x-1)**b; A=exp(2*pi*I*a); B=exp(2*pi*I*b); Ginf=exp(-2*pi*I*(a+b)); simplify(Ginf*B*A-1)==0
checkable.asserts: For n=1 with y = x^a (x-1)^b, the local monodromies at 0, 1 and infinity multiply to the identity (rank-one instance of the relation (G)...(B)(A) = (0)).

checkable.sympy: from sympy import *; A=Matrix(2,2,symbols('A11 A12 A21 A22')); B=Matrix(2,2,symbols('B11 B12 B21 B22')); y=Matrix(symbols('y1 y2')); expand((A*(B*y)) - (A*B)*y)==zeros(2,1)
checkable.asserts: Continuing around a (y -> A y) and then substituting the b-monodromy into the original branches gives the composite matrix A*B, illustrating the order convention behind Riemann's (B)(A).
